## Setup

```{r}
#| label: 0_library-imports

library(tidyverse)
```

Bringing in data exported from the BiosphereFutures database. I name my export files by date (in YYMMDD format); here, `export-date` determines which file we want to read from.

```{r}
#| label: 0_import-bf-data

export.date <- "261013"
export.filename <- paste0("~/CatStat/Data/Scenarios-Export-", export.date, ".csv")
bf <- read.csv(export.filename, header=TRUE)
```

It's nice to change the column names to be shorter and more manageable. In doing so, it's necessary to consider that the export file's column names might be in an unexpected order. `match` and `gsub` help us handle that possibility.

```{r}
#| label: 0_arrange-file-columns

colnames.og <- c("ID", "Thematic page(s)", "Title", "Permalink", "Date Contributed", "Region", "Country", "Subnational Region", "Latitude", "Longitude", "Case Contributor", "Contributor Role", "Project Website", "Intro", "Description", "Impact", "Project Year", "Time Horizon", "Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)", "Ecosystem(s)", "Scale", "Method(s)", "Output(s)", "Participants included", "Theme(s)", "IPBES Scenario Type(s)", "Resource 1 (Reference)", "Resource 1 (Link)", "Resource 2 (Reference)", "Resource 2 (Link)", "Resource 3 (Reference)", "Resource 3 (Link)")

# The import process converts the parentheses in the column names to periods. So I'll repeat that conversion for my column name vector

colnames.og <- gsub("[\\(\\) ]", ".", colnames.og) 

# We'll reorder the column names in case the file has a different order. 

# I find the column order in a roundabout way to guard against the case where the file does not contain all of the columns listed above

# Actually it doesn't seem necessary to invert the order. I've commented out that part

colnames.order <- match(names(bf), colnames.og)

#colnames.order <- match( C(1:length(colnames.order.inv)), colnames.order.inv)

colnames.short <- c("id", "thm.pg", "title", "link", "date", "region", "country", "subnat", "lat", "lon", "case.contributor", "contributor.role", "website", "intro", "desc", "impact", "year", "horizon", "sdgs", "eco", "scale", "methods", "outputs", "participants", "themes", "ipbes.type", "ref1", "ref1.link", "ref2", "ref2.link", "ref3", "ref3.link")

names(bf) <- colnames.short[colnames.order]
```

# Topic 1: First steps

My goal for this topic is to import the BF data, wrangle it into a tidy format (meaning a format legible to R's visualization processes), and plot the proportion of cases that tick the various options of our categorical variables.

A note on terminology:

- Case: The BF database consists of 150+ "cases," each of which corresponds to a scenario planning study.

- Field: I use the term "field" to refer to the different variables tracked in the database. Title, year, date contributed, scale(s), and region are fields. I may use this term interchangeably with "variable."

- Option: By definition, our categorical fields consist of various options that might apply to a given case. The SDG field has 17 options (for the 17 SDGs), our Region field has 7 options (including non-selection), etc. I refer to a case as "ticking" the options that apply to it. I may use this term interchangeably with "value."

- Multiple-select vs single-choice: I refer to fields in which multiple options can be ticked as "multiple-select" fields. Variables for which only one option can be chosen are "single-choice" fields.

## What I did

**Setting up the data**

The multiple-select fields are:

|                                 |                       |
|---------------------------------|-----------------------|
| Sustainable Development Goal(s) | Ecosystem(s)          |
| Scale(s)                        | Method(s)             |
| Output(s)                       | Participants included |
| IPBES Scenario Type(s)          |                       |

(Note: Theme(s) and Thematic page(s) might also be in this category, but I'm excluding them for now because they're optional)

```{r}
#| label: 1_setup-multi-fields

fields.multi <- c("sdgs", "eco", "scale", "methods", "outputs", "participants", "ipbes.type")
source("1_multiselect_to_binary.R")
bf.multi <- multi_occ(bf, fields.multi, missing = TRUE, shorten = TRUE)
```

The single-choice variables are Region and Contributor Role

(Note: Although "Country" and "Project year" could also hypothetically be represented as single-choice variables, the possible options are not (usefully) bounded.

```{r}
#| label: 1_setup-single-fields

fields.single <- c("region", "contributor.role")
source("1_tidy_singlechoice.R")
# bf.single is defined in the script sourced above.

bf.choice <- cbind(bf.multi, bf.single)
```

**Finding the proportions**

To find the proportion of cases that tick each variable option, I applied different procedures for the multiple-select and single-choice fields. For the multiple-select variables, the proportions can be found using `mean`, since they are represented by 0s and 1s. For the single-choice variables, we can use `count()` and divide by the total number of cases.

When finding the proportions for each field, I had to decide whether to include cases missing data for that field (or `NA` values) in the total count. I decided not to include `NA`s for the multiple-select fields, because missing data usually means that the field wasn't available on the contribution form for that case. True non-selection is represented by `0` instead. For the single-choice fields (specifically region, here, as there are no `NA`s for contributor role), `NA` refers to purposeful non-selection, so I decided to include them in the count.

We set our threshold for notable rarity at **5%**

For the error bars, I found confidence intervals using the Wilson Score Interval, as implemented in the `npsm::wilson.ci()` method. Among confidence interval methods that presuppose the binomial distribution[^1], score interval approaches are best for small datasets. They find the interval by calculating the range of null hypotheses (assumed population proportions) for which the sample proportion would be reasonably likely (i.e. within a determined confidence level). I use the Wilson test specifically because it was suggested in [Agresti 2018](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-introductory-statistics/an-introduction-to-categorical-data-analysis-3rd-edition-p-9781119405283).

[^1]: the equivalent of the normal distribution for binary data in which individual observations can be assumed to be independent of each other. "Observations," here, means ticks for a given option between cases. More on this in the Questions section.

We set our confidence level at 95%.

```{r}
#| label: 1_highlight-low-proportions

lowprop <- 0.05 # The threshold for which proportions we consider "low"
conf <- .95 # Desired confidence level for confidence interval (1 - alpha)

source("1_plot_proportions.R")
bf.prop <- bf.choice |> 
  find_all_multi_proportions(fields.multi, fields.single) |>
  find_prop_CI(conf)

bf.low <- bf.prop |> select(field, option, prop) |> filter(prop < lowprop)
bf.low
```

## Discussion

There are no real surprises on the low-proportion options. It's perhaps interesting that the "Open waters" ecosystem (sea) is *so* much rarer than "Coastal and marine areas" (cst), but it makes sense that scenario planning efforts would focus more on areas that have more human presence (even though human activity certainly has material impacts on remote areas as well).

I was surprised at the very different distribution of methods among cases set in International Waters (or that didn't choose a region) - until I remembered that those regions are low-proportion. It's probably best to understand that particular variance as noise, stemming from the fact that those regions are dominated by, like, 3 studies each. This dynamic also holds for outputs and participants. There's a lot more variation between regions for ecosystems and scales. For SDGs, there was obvious variation for the Europe and Central Asia region: the proportions of SDG 11 and 13 in this region even sit outside the error bars for the other regions.

I'll note that confidence intervals on contributor role don't mean anything, right? Among the broader population of scenario planning case studies (not yet submitted to the BF database), the "contributor role" variable has no value, because there is not yet a contributor. In other words, this variable only applies to cases that have already been sampled - there is no "population" proportion.

## Questions and next Steps

To get the options displayed in the right order, I'd need to recode the data as factors. I don't know what impact that will have on all the code I've written.

I'm concerned about how long it takes for R to process my code, especially since I'm not doing anything particularly complex. Is there anything obvious I can do to make my code less expensive?

Is it alright to use the binomial distribution (for my CI calculation)? The binomial distribution requires the "observations" (the cases, here) be independent of each other. It is clear that independence does not hold between options: we have seen correlations both within (e.g. between the "mapping" and "modelling" methods) and between (e.g. the "mapping" method and the "maps" output) fields. It might be possible that the cases have some dependence too - for example, one could argue that a high profile case being submitted to the database could encourage people doing similar work to submit their cases. Or, more straightforwardly, one could point to the influx of UREx, Radical Ocean Futures, or African Futures cases. However, I don't know how to proceed with analysis without assuming independence anyway.

How does the non-randomness of our dataset affect my CI considerations?

Is there anything I need to worry about, regarding my decisions to ignore or not ignore `NA`s for the single-choice and multiple-select data, respectively?

## Appendix

You can find my code on [Github](https://github.com/LiamCU1/CatStat). The following scripts are relevant:

- 1_multiselect_to_binary.R contains all my wrangling of the multiple-select data (into columns for each option, in which "ticks" are represented by 1s (and non-ticks are 0s).

```{r}
#| echo: fenced

# highlight

# field: a string which must be one of the column names defined above
# missing: binary, determines whether function will add a column of 0s for missing values
# shorten: binary, determines whether value names will be shortened in output df
# returns a data frame containing binary-presence data for each 
# value of field per record
occ <- function(bfdat, field, missing = FALSE, shorten = TRUE){
  bf_f <- bfdat |>
    select(id, matches(field))
  names(bf_f)[2] <- "f"
  bf_f <- bf_f |>
    mutate(field_split = strsplit(f, split = "|", fixed = TRUE)) |> #mutate adds another column with the split values
    mutate(f = NULL) |>
    unnest(field_split, keep_empty = TRUE) |> # unnest creates a new row for 
    # each value in the field list
    mutate(value = 1) # this is preparation for the pivot - because I'm looking for 
  # simple binary-presence data, there's no "value" to feed into pivot_wider. 
  # I've appended a column of 1s so that it has at least that
  
  na.ids <- filter(bf_f, is.na(field_split))[["id"]] # Record NA rows for later
  bf_f <- bf_f |> filter_out(is.na(field_split)) |> 
    pivot_wider(names_from = field_split, values_fill = 0)
  
  # Now we'll bring in the value names
  valnm <- import_value_names(field, fields.filenames)
  valnm.og <- valnm[["orig"]]
  valnm.sht <- valnm[["short"]]
  
  bf_fnoid <- bf_f |> mutate(id = NULL)
  valnm.order <- match(valnm.og, names(bf_fnoid))
  
  # Check if there are any possible values not present in the data
  if(NA %in% valnm.order){
    missind <- which(valnm.order %in% NA) # indices of missing values
    missvals <- valnm.og[missind]
    if(missing){
      # add column of 0s
      for(val in missvals){
        bf_fnoid <- bf_fnoid |> mutate("{val}" := 0)
      }
    }else{
      # remove missing value from valnm
      valnm.og <- valnm.og[! missind]
      valnm.sht <- valnm.sht[! missind]
    }
  }
  bf_fnoid <- bf_fnoid[valnm.og] # reorder columns
  
  if(shorten){
    names(bf_fnoid) <- paste0(field, ".", valnm.sht)
  }
  
  bf_fnas <- occ_nas(na.ids, colnames(bf_fnoid))
  
  bf_f <- cbind(bf_f["id"], bf_fnoid)
  bf_f <- rbind(bf_f, bf_fnas) |> arrange(id)
  
  return(bf_f)
}
```

- 1_tidy_singlechoice.R contains my wrangling for the single-choice data. This entirely means shortening the names for the region options.

  ```{r}
  #| echo: fenced

  # highlight

  tidy_singles <- function(bfdat, long, short){
  for(i in 1:length(long)){
    bfdat[bfdat == long[i]] <- short[i]
  }
  return(bfdat)
  ```

- 1_plot_proportions.R handles the proportion and confidence interval calculations

  ```{r}
  #| echo: fenced

  # highlight

  find_multifield_proportions <- function(bfdat, field){
    field.pre <- paste0(field, ".")
    bf.f <- bfdat |> select(starts_with(field.pre))
    # Exclude NAs in count. For any record, any option being NA means all must be
    f1 <- names(bf.f)[1]
    field.n <- bf.f |> filter(!is.na(.data[[f1]])) |> nrow()
    props <- bf.f |> summarise(across(everything(), 
                                      ~mean (.x, na.rm = TRUE)))
    
    props <- props |> pivot_longer(starts_with(field.pre), names_to = "option", 
                                   names_prefix = field.pre, values_to = "prop") |>
      mutate(field = field, .before = option) |> 
      mutate(n = field.n, .before = option)
    
    return(props)
  }

  find_prop_CI <- function(bfprops, conf){
    bfprops <- bfprops |> mutate(ct = prop * n) |> 
      rowwise() |> mutate(ci = list(wilson.ci(ct, n, conf.level = conf)), 
                          ci.low = ci[[1]], ci.hi = ci[[2]]) |>
      mutate(ct = NULL, ci = NULL)
    return(bfprops)
  }
  ```

# Topic 2: Contingency Tables

My goal for this topic is to perform independence tests, calculate residuals, and make mosaic plots for both my single-choice and multiple-response data.

Another note on terminology: in their text about the MRCV (multiple-response categorical variables) R package, Koziol and Bilder (2014) use the word "item" to describe the options within a multiple-response variable. I will adopt that language from now.

## What I did

First, I added a decade variable to the single choice table, using `cut()` to convert the "year" variable into an ordered factor. I added a function to `1_tidy_singlechoice.R` to handle this.

Then I created a contingency table for region and decade. I verified that this looks as expected in the console. I'll apply a X^2^ test of independence. Here, this test's null hypothesis assumes that the cells are independent of each other: that, in the broader population of potential cases, the probability that a case was conducted in Africa in the 2010s is determined fully by (a) how many cases were conducted in the 2010s, and (b) how many cases were conducted in Africa. We find:

```{r}
source("2_single-choice_mosaic.R")
single.test.vars <- c("decade", "region")
bf.single |> singles_x2_test(single.test.vars)
```

Although this X-squared value may seem large, our 3 x 7 table has many degrees of freedom. According to [this table](https://numiqo.com/tutorial/chi-square-distribution), the critical value (with a confidence level of 95%) for 12 degrees of freedom is \~ X^2^ = 21. So we do not reject the null hypothesis for these variables - there is no evidence of a statistically significant relationship.

The `chisq.test()` function throws a warning because there are cells in the contingency table with a count lower than 5. These are the previously noted low-proportion region items ("International Waters" and "None"), as well as a new low-proportion decade item (the 2000s). What happens if I combine the 2000s with the 2010s?

```{r}
library(forcats)

bf.single.combinedec <- bf.single |> mutate(decade = fct_collapse(decade, 
                                   before2020 = c("2000s", "2010s")))

bf.single.combinedec |> singles_x2_test(single.test.vars)
  
```

Here we get a lower X^2^ value of 7.666. Because the lower number of rows decreases the degrees of freedom (df = 6), and the higher cell counts increase the power, the p-value is actually lower than before at `p = 0.2636`. This still isn't enough evidence to reject the independence hypothesis.

What happens when we look at the multiple-response variables?

The `MRCV` (multiple response categorical variables) package enables independence tests on multiple-response data by creating larger contingency tables (in which each cell becomes a 2x2 table, relating the presence/absence of the row item to the presence/absence of the column item) and adapting the basic statistical tests to account for the extra complexity. Normal independence tests do not apply to multiple-response data because these tests do not account for the dependencies that likely exist within variables in MRCV data.

For now, I'll use their Rao-Scott adjustment, since I think our dataset is too small for bootstrapping to be the best option.

We apply the independence test to the IPBES type (row) and the Methods (column).

```{r}
source("2_mrcv_test.R")
mrtestvars <- c("ipbes.type", "methods")

bf.ipb.method.test <- bf.choice |> bf_mrcv_test(mrtestvars)

bf.ipb.method.test$rs2$S.rs2
bf.ipb.method.test$rs2$p.value.rs2
```

We get a X^2^ value of \~27.4 (df \~ 14), which is above the critical value of 26.8. The p-value is \~.0014, prompting us to reject the independence hypothesis for these variables: it appears that studies do choose their methods based on their intended intervention in the policy cycle. Makes sense.

How would it come out different if we naively applied the normal independence test to multiple-response data? Let's try it with IPBES type and method. I'll use `MRCV::marginal.table()` to create a "normal" contingency table to perform the test on.

```{r}

bf.ipb.method.marginal <- bf.choice |> 
  select(starts_with(mrtestvars)) |> na.omit() |> data.matrix() |>
  crossprod()

# Make sure there are no repeat items between rows and cols

Inum <- bf.choice |> select(starts_with(mrtestvars[1])) |> ncol()

bf.ipb.method.naive <- bf.ipb.method.marginal[1:Inum, -(1:Inum)] |> 
  chisq.test()

paste0("X^2 = ", bf.ipb.method.naive$statistic)
paste0("p = ", bf.ipb.method.naive$p.value)
```

The naive version of the test gives a X^2^ value \~20.3. With 18 degrees of freedom, that only gives a p-value = 0.315, which is far too large to reject the null hypothesis at 95% confidence. It seems the MRCV package's independence test is more likely to lead us to reject H_0 than a naive application of a chi-squared test.

We've tested whether these cases' proportions of methods are independent of their IPBES type (likely not), but I'm also curious whether a case's methods choices can be considered independent of its other methods. We know that there are patterns in the methods (e.g. cases that use modelling are also likely to use mapping), but I wonder if we can use `MI.test()` to see if there's a significant relationship.

Answer: we can't, really. `MI.test()` needs the names of the data frame's columns to be unique. And when I adapted the functions I wrote to get around that, I got absurd values like p = 6e-11. I don't think I understand how or why that happened. If I had to guess, though, it's something to do with the degrees of freedom in that test being 2, likely because the item-response table is mirrored across the diagonal. But I don't know.

Leaving the code as-is below. The modified MRCV test function code will be commented out in `2_mrcv_test.R`.

## Discussion

The mosaic plot is more or less what we'd expect. The number of cases per region doesn't change very much before/after 2020, except that we saw a dramatic increase in cases focusing on International Waters. However, that dramatic increase is from 1 case to 5 cases (should probably be 6, but Radical Ocean Futures doesn't have a region right now). A quintupling is enough to trigger a statistically significant residual in the math, but that does seem like an artifact of how few International Waters cases we have in general. I think we can safely call Region and Decade independent.

(The mosaic is a bit ugly with the title overlapping the column labels, but just rotating the labels took me almost an hour, I decided moving the title isn't worth my time right now)

The ComplexUpset plot is pretty interesting. With how much "Workshop" dominates the dataset, it's interesting that the method is deployed on its own in only 10% of the data set (still the most common intersection, but not by very much). It's also interesting to see that if a method wasn't deployed in tandem with a workshop, it was almost always because it was in tandem with surveys or (less commonly) models. The 4 exception cases were either art-based methods, desktop studies, or both. These intersections seem to indicate several very different kinds of "workshop" underlying the workshop category - that might be worth looking closer at.

## Appendix

1.  1_tidy_singlechoice.R now creates a "decade" column as well.

    ```{r}
    #| echo: fenced

    # Takes: a column of years (string or numeric)
    # Returns: a column of decades (factors)
    years_to_decades <- function(years){
      decade.levels <- c("2000s", "2010s", "2020s")
      d.breaks <- c(2000, 2010, 2020, 2030)
      
      decades <- years |> as.numeric() |> 
        cut(breaks = d.breaks, labels = decade.levels, right = FALSE)
      
      return(decades)
    }
    ```

2.  2_single-choice.mosaic.R just calculates contingency tables and passes them on to `vcd::mosiac()` or `chisq.test()`

```{r}
#| echo: fenced

# vars: a character vector of length 2, naming the variables we want to cross-tabulate
# var order: c(<rows>, <columns>)
# outputs: a contingency table
singles_contingency2 <- function(bfdata, vars){
  vformula <- paste0(vars, collapse = " + ")
  xformula <- as.formula(paste("~", vformula))
  return(xtabs(xformula, bfdata))
}

# outputs: an object, the output of a chi squared test
singles_x2_test <- function(bfdata, vars){
  xt <- singles_contingency2(bfdata, vars)
  return(chisq.test(xt))
}

# outputs: a plot object, giving a mosaic test with the specifications given below
singles_mosaic <- function(bfdata, vars){
  xt <- singles_contingency2(bfdata, vars)
  xr <- chisq.test(xt)$stdres
  p <- mosaic(xt, gp = shading_Friendly, residuals = xr, 
              residuals_type = "Std\nresiduals", labeling = labeling_border(rot_labels = c(90,0,0,90), 
                                                                            just_labels = c("left", "center", "center", "center")))
  return(p)
}

```

3.  2_mrcv_test.R passes on data to the core functions from `MRCV`

```{r}

#| echo: fenced

# bfdata = data frame in observation format (0s and 1s for mrcvs)
# vars = character vector, giving the names of 2 variables to be compared
# returns item response table
bf_mrcv_irtable <- function(bfdata, vars){
  Inum <- bfdata |> select(starts_with(vars[1])) |> ncol()
  Jnum <- bfdata |> select(starts_with(vars[2])) |> ncol()
  bf.ir <- bfdata |> select(starts_with(vars)) |>
    item.response.table(Inum, Jnum)
  return(bf.ir)
}

# bfdata = data frame in observation format (0s and 1s for mrcvs)
# vars = character vector, giving the names of 2 variables to be compared
# test.type = string specifying testing approach (see MRCV::MI.test)
# returns marginal independent test results for vars in vars
bf_mrcv_test <- function(bfdata, vars, test.type = "rs2"){
  Inum <- bfdata |> select(starts_with(vars[1])) |> ncol()
  Jnum <- bfdata |> select(starts_with(vars[2])) |> ncol()
  bf.test <- bfdata |> select(starts_with(vars)) |> 
    MI.test(Inum, Jnum, type = test.type)
  return(bf.test)
}

```

4.  2_upset.R formats data for the ComplexUpset graph and passes it on

```{r}

#| echo: fenced

# bfdata = data frame in observation format (0s and 1s)
# field = string specifying which MR variable to plot intersections of
# min.size, num.intersectinos, keep_empty_groups: parameters for ComplexUpset::upset
# Returns a ComplexUpset plot of the intersectinos for field
bf_mr_upset <- function(bfdata, field, min.size = 0, num.intersections = NULL, keep_empty_groups = FALSE){
  # Working on a subset of rows that are complete
  bf.up <- bfdata |> select(starts_with(field)) |> na.omit() |> 
    mutate(across(everything(), ~ .x == 1)) # converting 0s and 1s to binary
  items <- bf.up |> colnames()
  p <- upset(bf.up, items, name = field, min_size = min.size, 
             n_intersections = num.intersections, keep_empty_groups = keep_empty_groups)
  return(p)
}

```
